meanings: links a modifier to a noun

components.note: 白 (white, bright) — 的 first meant bright and clear, as in 的确 dí què.
勺 (sháo) is a loose sound clue for dì; 勺 also sounds out 约 yuē and 钓 diào.

example.fact: 的 is the most frequent character in written Chinese. It links a modifier to a noun (我的书 'my book'), and it can also stand in for the noun itself: 我的 means 'mine'. In the 是…的 pattern it stresses details such as when or how something happened.

components.note: 戈 (halberd) — a weapon radical, as in 战 war and 成. 我 began as a picture of a jagged-bladed weapon; the pronoun "I" is a later borrowing of the sound.

example.fact: Add 们 to make 我们 'we'. 我们 can include the listener, while 咱们 explicitly does (mainly in northern speech). Chinese often drops 我 when the subject is obvious, so a bare 想去 can already mean 'I want to go'.

components.note: 亻 (person) — marks people, as in 他 he, 们 plural, 住 live; 你 is "you".
尔 (ěr) is a loose sound clue for nǐ; 尔 also supplies 您 nín (polite you, with 心 added).

example.fact: 你 is the informal 'you'; the polite form is 您 (nín), which adds 心 'heart' below. Use 您 for elders, customers and strangers of higher status. Plural is 你们, and written Chinese uses 你 for both men and women.

components.note: 日 (sun) — on top; the usual explanation is sun over 正 "straight, correct": what is clear and straight is "right, is". A memory aid, not firm etymology.

example.fact: 是 links nouns (我是学生) but is NOT used before most adjectives: say 他很高, not 他是高. Answering yes/no questions, Chinese echoes the verb: 你是学生吗？— 是 means 'yes'.

components.note: 子 (child) — 了 is usually read as a swaddled baby, like 子 without the arms. Its meanings 'finish' (了解 liǎo) and the particle le were borrowed later.

example.fact: 了 marks a completed action after a verb (吃了) or a new situation at the end of a sentence (下雨了 'it's raining now'). It is not simply a past tense: 明天我吃了饭就去 uses it for a future completed step. Read as liǎo it means 'to finish', as in 了解.

examples.pinyin: Wàimiàn xiàyǔ le, dài sǎn ba.
examples.english: It's raining outside, take an umbrella.

examples.pinyin: Zuótiān wǒ mǎile yí jiàn yīfu.
examples.english: I bought a piece of clothing yesterday.

components.note: 一 (line) — dictionary reads 不 as a bird flying up toward the sky 一. The meaning 'not' is a borrowing, so the shape does not explain it today.
杯 (bēi) — a character that uses 不 as a loose sound clue (木 + 不). The sound is a hint only: 不 bù vs bēi.

example.fact: 不 turns into bú before a fourth-tone syllable: bú shì, bú qù. It negates present and future (我不去) while 没 negates 'have' and past events (我没去). The tone change is shown in pinyin but the character stays the same.

components.note: 土 (earth) — ground and place, as in 地 earth, 坐 sit; 在 is "to be at a place".
才 (cái) is a close sound clue for zài; 才 also appears in 材 cái.

example.fact: 在 works three ways: as a verb ('to be located', 他在家), as a preposition before a place (在北京工作), and as a progressive marker before a verb (我在吃饭 'I'm eating'). Put 在+place BEFORE the verb, unlike English.

components.note: 亻 (person) — marks people, as in 你 you, 们 plural, 做 do; 他 is "he" (or other).
也 (yě) is only a loose sound hint for tā; the sibling 她 tā (she) shares it with 女 for woman.

example.fact: 他, 她 and 它 sound identical (tā) and differ only in writing, so spoken Chinese has no he/she distinction. 他 historically served as a generic 'other (person)', and 他们 is still used for mixed or unspecified groups.

components.note: 戈 (halberd) — a weapon radical, as in 战 war and 成. 我 began as a picture of a jagged-bladed weapon; the pronoun "I" is a later borrowing of the sound.
亻 (person) — marks words about people, as in 你 you, 他 he, 做 do. Here it shows 们 pluralises person words (我们, 他们).
门 (mén) gives the sound: 们 is men (neutral tone), the same syllable as 门 gate.

example.fact: 们 attaches only to pronouns and words for people (我们, 你们, 朋友们) to mark plural — it can never attach to an ordinary object noun, so "books" is never 书们; Chinese instead relies on context or a number + measure word for object plurals.

examples.english: The teacher asked us to sit down first.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 她, 姐.
子 (child) — a woman with her child: the picture of something good.

example.english: The weather is very good today.
example.fact: 好 can sit before a verb to mean 'easy to': 好吃 'tasty', 好看 'nice-looking'. Spoken as 好 on its own it means 'OK'. It is also read hào ('to like') in words like 爱好, a different reading.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ hǎo, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ.

components.note: 月 (flesh/meat, not moon here) — oldest form is a hand holding a piece of meat, "to possess"; 月 as meat also appears in 肉 words like 肚 belly and 脑 brain.

example.fact: 有 is negated with 没, never 不: 我没有钱 'I have no money'. It also means 'there is': 桌子上有一本书. In Cantonese the same idea uses 冇 for 'not have', a character built from 有 by removing two strokes.

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì bēi chá.
examples.english: There is a cup of tea on the table.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement and place, as in 道 way, 过 pass, 近 near; the radical hints at "here / this way". The 文 part is not a useful sound clue.

example.fact: In speech 这 is often said zhèi, especially before a measure word (这个 zhèige). Before a number or measure word, use 这 + measure + noun: 这本书. Its partner is 那 (nà) 'that', and 这儿/这里 means 'here'.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bú shì wǒ de shǒujī.

components.note: 京 (jīng, high mound, capital) is a loose sound clue for jiù; going up to a high place fits 就 "to approach, to go to".

example.fact: 就 is a small adverb that links an earlier condition to a quick result: 一下课就回家 'go home as soon as class ends'. Compare 才 (cái), which suggests something happened later than expected: 他八点就到了 vs 他八点才到.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ chīwán fàn jiù qù túshūguǎn.
examples.english: I'll go to the library right after I eat.

components.note: 会 (meet, can) — simplified from 會, a lid on a container: bringing things together; hence meeting, then "can" (huì).

example.english: I can speak a little Chinese.
example.fact: 会 means 'can' for learned skills (会游泳 'can swim'), while 能 covers physical ability or permission. It also predicts the future: 明天会下雨 'it will probably rain'. The reading kuài shows up in 会计 'accountant'.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — speech sounds and particles: 吧, 呢, 吃; 吗 is the question particle.
马 (mǎ) sounds like 吗 (ma) — same syllable, different tone.

example.fact: 吗 turns any statement into a yes/no question: 你有钱。→ 你有钱吗？ It stays toneless. Do not add 吗 to a question that already has a question word (什么, 谁, 哪儿); 你是谁吗 would be wrong.

components.note: 要 (want, need) — oldest form shows hands at a waist: it meant "waist" (腰 yāo adds 月 flesh); "essential" followed.

example.english: I want a glass of water.
example.fact: 要 covers 'want', 'need' and 'will'; the negative of 'must' is 不用 or 别, not 不要 (which is 'don't want' or 'don't!'). It is the ancestor of the body-part character 腰 'waist', created by adding 月 'flesh'.

examples.english: Do you want tea or coffee?

components.note: 十 (shí, ten) is a loose sound clue for 什 (shén, shí in 什锦); old sense "a set of ten", hence "assorted". In 什么 it is simply "what".
幺 (tiny, a thread) — 么 looks like 幺 and was borrowed as a simplified form for the light particle in 什么, 怎么, 这么. The shape does not explain the meaning today.
厶 (loop) — the visible lower part, a small curl. Memory aid: a tiny stroke 丿 over a curl — a 'little something' you ask about: 什么 what?

example.fact: 什么 pairs with 都 (什么都可以, "anything is fine") to mean "anything at all" — one of several question words (谁, 哪里, 什么时候) that flip from a question word into an "any-" word simply by adding 都 after it.

examples.english: What dishes do you want to eat?

components.note: 讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 请, 谢, 话.
兑 (duì) is a loose sound clue for shuō; 兑 also sounds out 脱 tuō, 税 shuì and 悦 yuè.

example.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
example.fact: 说 also means 'to scold' (被老师说了) and, read shuì, 'to persuade' (游说). To repeat the verb with a degree complement, Chinese uses 说中文说得很好, as in the example.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 好, 姐; 她 is the female "she", coined to parallel 他.
也 (yě) is only a loose sound clue for tā; the 他 pair is the same part.

example.fact: 她 is a modern invention: the character became standard in the 1910s–20s, when writers wanted to translate European gendered pronouns. Before that, 他 covered both genders. Speech still has no he/she distinction, since both are tā.

components.note: 心 (heart) — thought and feelings, as in 思, 感, 急: to think of someone.
相 (xiāng) is a close sound clue for xiǎng; 相 also in 箱 xiāng and 湘 xiāng.

example.fact: 想 is a softer 'want' than 要: 我想喝茶 'I'd like tea'. It also means 'to think about' (想一想) and 'to miss' (我想你). Do not use it for 'think that' in a belief about facts; 我觉得 is more usual.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē yì bēi rèshuǐ.
examples.english: I'd like a cup of hot water.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.

example.fact: 一 changes tone: yí before a fourth tone (一个), yì before 1st–3rd tones (一杯). Alone, in counting or in a phone number it stays yī, and in phone numbers it is often said yāo to avoid confusion with 七 (qī).

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi rèshuǐ.
examples.english: Please give me a cup of hot water.

components.note: 彳 (step) — walking, as in 行, 往, 得.
艮 (gèn) is a close sound clue for hěn; 艮 also sounds out 跟 gēn, 根 gēn, 恨 hèn and 银 yín.

example.fact: Before a one-word adjective, 很 is often just a bridge, not 'very': 她很高 simply means 'She is tall'. Without 很, 她高 sounds like a comparison. For real intensity, stress it or use 非常 or 特别.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de cài hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: The food at this restaurant is delicious.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — knowing is something you can say aloud; 口 sits in many speech words (问 ask, 告 tell).
矢 (shǐ, arrow) is only a loose sound clue today; the same 知 sound is in 智 zhì (wisdom).
辶 (walk) — movement and roads, as in 这 this, 过 pass, 近 near; a 道 is a road, then a way or principle.
首 (shǒu, head) is only a loose sound hint for dào; 首 also means "head/first", fitting a lead-the-way road.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào tā de míngzi.
example.fact: 知道 ("to know" a fact or piece of information) is a common trap for English speakers, who have only one verb "to know" — Chinese requires 认识 instead for knowing a person, place, or being acquainted with something (认识他 "to know him", never 知道他).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zhīdào tā zhù zài nǎr.
Nǐ zhīdào xiànzài jǐ diǎn ma?
examples.english: Do you know what time it is?

components.note: 人 (person) — a side-view figure of a person walking. As a radical it appears as 亻 on the left: 你 他 们.

example.fact: 人 is a base of countless words: 中国人 'Chinese person', 好人 'good person'. It takes no measure word of its own in 人们 'people', and in counting it uses 个 or the polite 位: 三个人 / 三位客人.

examples.pinyin: Nà ge rén shì wǒmen de lǎoshī.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — speech sounds and particles: 吗, 呢, 啊; 吧 is a suggestion particle, or the bar in 酒吧.
巴 (bā) sounds exactly like 吧; also in 爸 bà, 把 bǎ, 爬 pá.

example.fact: 吧 softens requests and suggestions: 走吧 'let's go', 你来吧 'come on'. At the end of a statement it signals a guess: 他是老师吧？ 'He's a teacher, right?' It is toneless in this use but bā in the noun 酒吧 'bar'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiān chīfàn ba, bié děng wǒ.
examples.english: Go ahead and eat, don't wait for me.

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".

example.fact: Don't confuse 那 (nà, 'that') with 哪 (nǎ, 'which'): the second adds 口. 那 can also mean 'then, in that case' at the start of a reply: 那我们走吧 'Then let's go'. In speech it is often said nèi.

examples.pinyin: Nà shì nǐ de shǒujī ma?

examples.hanzi: 你不去的话，那我也不去。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bú qù dehuà, nà wǒ yě bú qù.
examples.english: If you're not going, then I won't go either.

meanings: used before a verb to show intent

components.note: 来 (come) — it began as a picture of a wheat plant; the sound was borrowed for "come". 麦 (wheat) still shows it, with a root 夂 added.

example.fact: 来 is the speaker-oriented 'come' and pairs with 去 'go'. As a verb ending it shows direction toward the speaker: 拿来 'bring'. 来 also stands in for specific verbs in offers, such as 我来 'let me do it'.

components.note: 阝 (city) — right-side 阝 is 邑 city — 都 is a capital, as in 首都; compare 那, 邮.
者 (zhě) — loose hint — 都 is dū; 者 also sounds out 赌 dǔ and 堵 dǔ, a dū/dǔ series.

example.fact: 都 'all' must come AFTER the thing it counts: 我们都去 (not 都我们去). It also means 'already': 都十二点了 'it's already twelve'. Read dū it means 'capital', as in 首都.

components.note: 人 (person) — the top part. 个 is the general measure word, as in 一个, 这个, 那个.
丨 (a vertical tally) — under 人, read as one tally mark per person: counting individuals one by one.

example.fact: 个 is the all-purpose measure word, used when you don't know the specific one. It is toneless in speech (liǎng ge). It simplifies the traditional 個, and the same shape is also an old standalone character.

components.note: 能 (can) — originally a picture of a bear, a strong animal (熊 xióng adds fire 灬); "strong, able" gave "can".

example.fact: 能 is 'can' by circumstance or ability: 我今天不能去 'I can't go today'. It differs from 会 (learned skill): 他会游泳, 但今天不能游 'he can swim, but can't today'. 能 also asks permission.

components.note: 土 (earth) — the top part, the ground family as in 地, 场, 块. Memory aid: leave the ground 土 and go off on your own 厶 path.
厶 (private, small loop) — the bottom part. Old forms show a person leaving a place, so the 土 story is only a mnemonic.

example.fact: 去 is movement away from the speaker, as 来 is toward. After a verb it marks direction away: 拿去 'take away'. A meaning 'last' appears in 去年 'last year'. Place words follow directly: 去北京, not 去到北京.

components.note: 氵 (water) — liquids and flowing; 没 first meant sink or submerge (淹没), which led to "gone" and then "not have".
殳 (shū) is only a loose sound hint for 没 (méi/mò); it also sits in 设 shè and 投 tóu.

example.fact: 没 negates 有 and past events: 我没去 'I didn't go'. Don't combine it with 了 in that case. Written 没有 in full, with 有 often dropped in speech. In 没 mò ('to sink') it is a different, rarer reading.

examples.english: I didn't go to work yesterday.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 口 is the mouth, as in 吃, 喝, 叫; 和 is harmony and speaking together.
禾 (hé) — same sound — 和 is hé, like 禾.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hé péngyou qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: I'm going to see a movie with a friend.
example.fact: 和 joins nouns only: 苹果和香蕉 'apples and bananas'. To join verbs or sentences use 而且 or just a comma. In Taiwan 和 in this sense is often said hàn. It also forms 和平 'peace' and 和气 'friendly'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé māma yìqǐ mǎi cài.
examples.english: I buy groceries with my mom.

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shang yǒu píngguǒ hé xiāngjiāo.
examples.english: There are apples and bananas on the table.

components.note: 亻 (person) — marks people, as in 你 you, 们 plural, 做 do; 他 is "he" (or other).
也 (yě) is only a loose sound hint for tā; the sibling 她 tā (she) shares it with 女 for woman.
亻 (person) — marks words about people, as in 你 you, 他 he, 做 do. Here it shows 们 pluralises person words (我们, 他们).
门 (mén) gives the sound: 们 is men (neutral tone), the same syllable as 门 gate.

example.english: They are studying in the library.
example.fact: Chinese had no gendered third-person pronoun at all until the early 20th century, when 她 (with the 女 radical) was introduced under the influence of Western literary translation to distinguish "she" from "he" — 他们 as the default, mixed-gender "they" still reflects that older, ungendered system.

components.note: 至 (arrive) — 到 is to arrive.
刂 is the knife form 刀 (dāo), a close sound clue for dào; 到 itself sounds out 倒 dǎo/dào.

example.fact: 到 can follow another verb to show the result is reached: 找到 'find (successfully)', 看到 'catch sight of', 买到 'manage to buy'. As a preposition it means 'to': 从八点到九点 'from 8 to 9'.

examples.english: What time do you get to the office?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān zǒu dào shí diǎn.
examples.english: Yesterday I walked until ten o'clock.

components.note: 寸 (hand, inch) — hands and measuring, as in 寻 seek, 导 lead, 射 shoot; 对 faces someone or matches a pair. 又 here only stands in for the left side of 對.

example.fact: 对 is the quick 'right/correct' reply: 对！ 'Exactly!'. As a preposition it means 'towards' or 'about': 他对我很好 'He is nice to me'. 对不起 'sorry' literally means 'can't face (you)'.

examples.pinyin: Duì, nǐ shuō de yìdiǎn yě méi cuò.
examples.english: Right, you're not wrong at all.

examples.pinyin: Tā duì wǒmen dōu hěn hǎo.
examples.english: He is very kind to all of us.

components.note: 也 (also) — began as a picture (a vessel or snake; scholars disagree) and was borrowed for 'also'. A loose sound clue in 他 tā, 她 tā, 地 dì, 池 chí.

example.fact: 也 goes before the verb, never at the end: 我也是学生. In negatives it means 'either': 我也不去. Pair 也 with 都 as 也都 in that order ('also all'), not 都也.

examples.pinyin: Tā bú qù, wǒ yě bù dǎsuàn qù.
examples.english: He's not going, and I don't plan to go either.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech, sounds and eating, as in 叫 call, 吃 eat, 唱 sing; 啊 is an exclamation.
阿 (ā) — same sound: 啊 ā.

example.fact: 啊 changes sound to blend with the previous word's ending: after -n it becomes na (难啊 nán na), after -i it becomes ya (是啊 shì ya), and it is sometimes written 呀 or 哇. It can express warmth, surprise or mild urging.

examples.pinyin: Shì a, wǒ yě zhème xiǎng.
Nǐ zěnme hái méi zǒu a?

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 过, 近, 送: 还 is to go back or return (huán), then "still" (hái).
不 here stands in for 睘 (huán) in the traditional 還, so it is not a real clue; same stand-in in 环 huán.

example.fact: 还 has two readings: hái 'still, also' (还没吃 'haven't eaten yet') and huán 'to return': 还钱 'pay back money'. The adverb hái also compares: 比这个还好 'even better than this'.

examples.english: What else would you like to eat?

meanings: marks the object before a verb
measure word for things with a handle

components.note: 扌 (hand) — marks actions done by hand, as in 打, 拉, 提; 把 is to grasp.
巴 (bā) gives the sound: 把 bǎ is close, as in 爸 bà and 吧 ba.

example.fact: The 把 construction moves the object before the verb: 我把书放在桌子上 'I put the book on the table'. It focuses on what's done to the object, so the verb needs a result, e.g. 关上 or 放在. 把 is also a measure word for chairs and knives.

examples.hanzi: 我把手机放在桌子上了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ shǒujī fàng zài zhuōzi shang le.
examples.english: I put my phone on the table.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zuòyè jiāo gěi lǎoshī.
examples.english: Please hand your homework in to the teacher.

components.note: 讠 (speech, simplified 言) — words and talk, as in 说 say, 请 please.
上 (shàng) is only a stand-in with the same rhyme -ang; the traditional 讓 used 襄 xiāng, also in 嚷 rǎng and 壤 rǎng.

example.english: Mom told me to go to bed early.
example.fact: 让 means 'to let' or 'to have someone do': 让我看看 'let me see'. In a passive-like sentence it can mark the doer: 书让他拿走了 'the book was taken by him'. Its original meaning 'to yield' survives in 让座 'give up one's seat'.

examples.english: Please let me take a look.

examples.pinyin: Bié ràng háizi yí ge rén qù.
examples.english: Don't let the child go alone.

components.note: 亻 (person radical, 单人旁) — people and what they do: 你, 他, 作. 做 is a later variant of 作 zuò (to do), sharing its meaning and sound.
故 (gù) is only a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 做 is the everyday 'do/make': 做饭 'cook', 做作业 'do homework'. It is a later variant of 作, which still appears in written compounds such as 工作 and 作者. 做 is preferred for hands-on tasks.

examples.english: She wants to be a teacher.

components.note: 纟 (thread, simplified 糸) — silk and cord: 红, 线, 组; 给 is to supply thread, then to give.
合 (hé) is only a loose sound clue; same part in 答 dá, 拾 shí, 恰 qià.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.
example.fact: 给 can be 'to give' (我给你) or a preposition 'for/to': 给我打电话 'call me'. After another verb it marks the recipient: 送给她 'give to her'. Read jǐ in compounds like 供给 'to supply'.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi bīngshuǐ.
examples.english: Please give me a glass of iced water.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
人 (person) — the top part. 个 is the general measure word, as in 一个, 这个, 那个.
丨 (a vertical tally) — under 人, read as one tally mark per person: counting individuals one by one.

example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu yí gè píngguǒ.
example.english: There is an apple on the table.
example.fact: 个 is Mandarin's default "general" measure word — when a noun's own specific classifier is unknown, forgotten, or simply doesn't exist, 个 is always a safe substitute, making 一个 one of the first and most reusable phrases a learner picks up.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yí ge xīn shǒujī.
examples.english: I want to buy a new phone.

examples.pinyin: Tā yí ge rén zhù zài zhèlǐ.

components.note: 上 (above) — a mark above a line, the mirror of 下 below.

example.english: The book is on the table.
example.fact: 上 appears after a noun as 'on/above': 桌子上 'on the table'. It can mean 'previous': 上个月 'last month', and 上班 'go to work', 上学 'go to school'. Its opposite is 下.

examples.pinyin: Shàng ge xīngqī wǒ hěn máng.
examples.english: I was very busy last week.

components.note: 亻 (person) — marks people, as in 他 he, 们 plural, 住 live; 你 is "you".
尔 (ěr) is a loose sound clue for nǐ; 尔 also supplies 您 nín (polite you, with 心 added).
亻 (person) — marks words about people, as in 你 you, 他 he, 做 do. Here it shows 们 pluralises person words (我们, 他们).
门 (mén) gives the sound: 们 is men (neutral tone), the same syllable as 门 gate.

example.english: What would you all like to drink?
example.fact: English "you" is ambiguous between one person and a group, but Mandarin marks the distinction explicitly: 你 is always singular and 你们 is always plural, with no equivalent gap the way English relies on context or "you guys".

examples.english: What time will you arrive tomorrow?
Thank you all for your help.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 这, 近, 送: 过 is to pass or cross.
寸 here replaces 咼 (guō) of the traditional 過, so it is not a sound clue; 咼 survives in 锅 guō and 祸 huò.

example.fact: After a verb, 过 shows experience: 我吃过 'I've eaten it before'. As a full verb it means 'to pass/spend': 过年 'celebrate the New Year', 过马路 'cross the road'. In the experience use it is toneless.

examples.english: Have you ever eaten Peking duck?

components.note: 氵 (water) — liquids and flowing; 没 first meant sink or submerge (淹没), which led to "gone" and then "not have".
殳 (shū) is only a loose sound hint for 没 (méi/mò); it also sits in 设 shè and 投 tóu.
月 (flesh/meat, not moon here) — oldest form is a hand holding a piece of meat, "to possess"; 月 as meat also appears in 肉 words like 肚 belly and 脑 brain.

example.english: There's no milk left in the fridge.
example.fact: 没 is the one verb that can negate 有 ("to have/there is") — Mandarin's everyday negator 不 cannot be used here (不有 is simply wrong), which is why 没有 has to be learned as its own fixed negation rather than 不 plus 有.

meanings: particle linking a verb to its result or degree

components.note: 彳 (step) — walking and going, as in 行, 往, 很 very.
寸 (hand) — oldest form is a hand grabbing a cowrie shell (money): 得 is "to obtain". The shell has worn down to 旦.

example.fact: 得 (de) links a verb to how well or how far it goes: 说得好 'speaks well'. The same character is dé in the sense 'to obtain' (得到) and děi 'must' (我得走). Each reading does a different job.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān lái de hěn zǎo.

components.note: 手 (hand) — over 目 (eye): a hand shading the eyes to look into the distance. 目 marks seeing words, as in 眼, 睡.

example.fact: 看 pictures a hand shading the eye. It covers 'look', 'watch' and 'read': 看书, 看电视. As a softener it means 'try': 尝尝看 'give it a taste'. Read kān it means 'to guard', as in 看守.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ juéde nǐ kàn cuò le.
